vignette:
At twenty-six, Samira has already built a life that looks steady from the outside. They live with their partner in a small apartment above a bakery, and they work long days as a veterinarian at a busy animal hospital. They are known at work for their calm hands with frightened animals, for kneeling on the floor to coax a trembling dog out from under a chair, for speaking gently even when the waiting room is chaotic. It is hard for people who meet them there to imagine how abruptly that sense of safety was broken.

The robbery happens late in the fall, after an evening shift that runs past closing. Samira leaves the clinic tired and hungry, still carrying the sharp smells of antiseptic and wet fur on their scrubs. They stop at an ATM a few blocks from the bus stop, thinking mostly about getting home and whether their partner is still awake. While they are putting their wallet away, a man comes up fast from behind and grabs at their bag. At first Samira thinks it is some kind of mistake. Then he shoves them hard enough that their shoulder hits the side of the machine. He tells them not to look at him. His voice is flat, close to their ear. Samira remembers the metallic taste that rises in their mouth, the cold air, the way their body seems to stop belonging to them. When they hesitate, he strikes them again and yanks the bag free. For a second they think he may have a knife, though later they are not sure if they actually saw one or only felt the certainty of it. What stays with them most clearly is not the loss of money or the phone but the helplessness of standing there while someone decides what happens to them.

In the first days afterward, Samira tries to treat the event like something unpleasant that should be put behind them. They file a police report, cancel cards, replace keys. They tell the story in a clipped, practical way, as if details can be organized into something manageable. But at night the memory comes back without warning. As they are drifting off, they feel again the impact of their shoulder against metal and hear the command not to look. They jolt awake with their heart racing, already sweating. Some nights they dream they are back at the ATM; other nights the dream shifts and the attacker’s face is replaced by strangers from the street or even by clients from the clinic. In the morning they are ashamed by how shaken they feel.

Soon they begin changing their routines. They refuse evening shifts if they can. If they have to stay late for an emergency surgery or a sick cat in labor, they ask their partner to pick them up and become tense if there is any delay. They avoid the block where the robbery happened, then avoid ATMs entirely, then start scanning every sidewalk on the walk from the bus. Their partner notices that Samira no longer wears headphones outside and checks the apartment locks repeatedly before bed. Even inside, they startle at footsteps on the stairs or the buzz of the intercom.

The fear follows them into work in ways that embarrass them. A large dog lunges suddenly off an exam table one afternoon, and Samira’s whole body reacts before they can think. They step back so quickly they knock over a tray of syringes. Their technician looks at them with concern, and Samira laughs it off, but their hands shake for the rest of the appointment. They begin to dread the unpredictability of the waiting room—the sudden barking, raised voices, men entering quickly through the front door. They are still tender with animals, still careful and competent, but it now costs them more. By the end of the day they feel wrung out, as if they have been holding every muscle braced for hours.

At home, their world grows smaller. Their partner suggests dinner with friends, a late movie, a walk after sunset, and Samira finds reasons to say no. They tell themselves they are tired from work. Sometimes that is true. More often, the thought of being outside after dark produces a rush of dread so immediate it feels like common sense rather than fear. They become irritable in ways that surprise them. When their partner forgets to text that they are running late, Samira snaps, then feels guilty and withdrawn. Physical closeness is complicated too. If their partner comes up behind them in the kitchen, Samira flinches hard enough to spill whatever they are holding. They both go quiet after moments like that.

What unsettles Samira most is how often the robbery is present when nothing visible is wrong. A stranger reaching into a pocket on the train, a man standing too close in line for coffee, the reflection of someone behind them in a dark window—each can pull them halfway back into that night before they have time to orient themselves. In those moments, their chest tightens, their hearing narrows, and their thoughts become simple and urgent: get out, don’t turn around, don’t let them near you. They know, rationally, that most people are not dangerous. They say this to themselves often. But their body does not believe it.

Months later, Samira speaks about the robbery with a mixture of precision and disbelief, as if recounting something both overfamiliar and still unresolved. They are frustrated by how much space it occupies in their life. They miss the version of themselves who moved through the city absentmindedly, who stayed late to help a sick animal without calculating the route home, who did not measure every doorway and every pair of footsteps. What they grieve, more than the stolen bag or bruises that faded quickly, is the ordinary confidence they once carried without noticing.
